lessons.title: Drawing types and scales
lessons.theory:
In engineering, most design information is shown on **drawings**. Today, drawings are generally produced on computer using **CAD (computer-aided design)** systems.

A key factor on a drawing is the **scale** - the size of items on the drawing in relation to their real size. When all items are shown relative to their real size, the drawing is a **scale drawing**. 

### Types of Drawings
* **General arrangement (GA)**: Show whole devices or structures using a small scale (e.g., 1:100).
* **Detail drawings**: Show parts in detail using a large scale (e.g., 1:5 or 1:2). Small parts are sometimes shown as **actual size** (1:1) or can be **enlarged** (e.g., 2:1).
* **Schematic drawings (schematics)**: Simplified forms used for electrical circuits and pipe networks (e.g., a map of a train network).

Note: 'Drawing' is often abbreviated to **dwg**.

exercises.question: Enlarged drawings show components larger than their ____.
exercises.hint: Refer to the size in real life.
exercises.explanation: Actual size (1:1) means the drawing is the same size as the real object. Enlarged means bigger.

exercises.hint: It relates the drawing size to real size.
exercises.explanation: Scale determines how much an object is reduced or enlarged on paper.

exercises.explanation: General arrangement (GA) drawings show the whole device or structure.

exercises.explanation: Schematics are simplified forms of networks or circuits.

exercises.explanation: A set of drawings consists of a number of related drawings.

exercises.question: Most drawings are produced on computers, using ____ software.
exercises.explanation: CAD stands for Computer-Aided Design.

lessons.title: Types of views used on drawings
lessons.theory:
Engineers use different **views** to visualize components from various angles:

* **Plan**: A view from above (looking down).
* **Elevation**: A view from the side (e.g., front elevation).
* **Section (cross-section)**: A view inside an object, as if it were cut through.
* **Exploded view**: A 3D view showing components spaced out (taken to pieces).
* **3D views**: Often shown as **oblique projections** or **isometric projections**.

Note: Two-dimensional and three-dimensional are often shortened to **2D** and **3D**.

lessons.title: Drawing terminology in context
lessons.theory: In professional conversations, engineers use specific terms to describe the drawings they need or are reviewing. They might discuss the **scale**, ask for a **section** to see internal details, or refer to a **schematic** for simplified networks.

exercises.question: We need a ____ through the bridge, showing the profile of the deck.
exercises.explanation: A section shows the internal profile.

exercises.question: The only drawing we have is the ____, which is 1:100, so it obviously doesn't show things in detail.
exercises.explanation: General arrangement (GA) drawings use small scales for overall views.

lessons.title: Initial design phase
lessons.theory:
The design process begins with a **design brief** – a list of essential requirements from the client. 

From this brief, designers create a **concept** (an overall design idea) and produce **rough sketches** (hand-drawn illustrations). As the design develops, these sketches are refined into **preliminary drawings** which can be assessed in more detail.

exercises.question: A description of design objectives is a ____.
exercises.hint: The first document from the client.
exercises.explanation: A design brief outlines the requirements for a project.

exercises.question: A rough, hand-drawn illustration is a ____.
exercises.explanation: Sketches are rough illustrations used in early stages.

exercises.question: An initial diagram, requiring further development, is a ____.
exercises.explanation: Preliminary drawings are developed from sketches.

exercises.question: An overall design idea is a ____.
exercises.explanation: A concept is the overall design idea.

lessons.title: Collaborative development
lessons.theory:
In large projects, drawings are **issued** or **circulated** (distributed) to the team. They are often **revised**, **amended**, or **redesigned** (changed) following comments. 

Each **revision** is numbered. For example, drawing 110A becomes 110B. Revision B is then the **current** drawing, and A is **superseded** (replaced). 

Once a preliminary drawing is approved, a senior engineer will **sign off** (authorize) it, turning it into a **working drawing** that the production or construction team can **work to**.

exercises.question: Match the verbs with similar meanings.

pairs.definition: Amend, Redesign, Refine, Revise
Circulate, Issue

exercises.explanation: These verbs describe different stages of managing drawings.

exercises.explanation: A draft is the initial version of a document.

lessons.theory: Each drawing has a revision history. When an **amendment** is made, the **revision** letter changes. **Notes** in the right-hand column detail the changes made. When a new version is **issued**, the previous one is **superseded**.

exercises.explanation: The current drawing is the one that should be used.

exercises.question: ...and I have therefore told the fabrication team not to ____ to it.
exercises.explanation: Teams work to current drawings.

lessons.title: Design objectives
lessons.theory:
A **design brief** for a **proposed** product consists of several key elements:

* **Function**: The product's intended use (what it is designed to do), including performance targets.
* **Constraints**: Limits on the design (e.g., maximum size or weight limit).
* **Comparative targets**: How well the product performs compared with **existing models**.
* **Design features**: Specific things the design must have (e.g., a lock).
* **Budget**: The cost limits that must not be exceeded to make the design **cost-effective**.

The goal is to produce a **design solution** that meets all technical objectives.

exercises.question: Cost limitations are always a ____!
exercises.explanation: Constraints are limits or restrictions on a design.

exercises.question: A ____ has been allocated for the preliminary design phase.
exercises.explanation: A budget is the allocated cost for a project.

exercises.question: But we mustn't ____ that amount.
exercises.explanation: Costs should not exceed the budget.

exercises.question: If we spend more than we earn, that's not a ____ design solution.
exercises.explanation: Cost-effective means producing a good result without wasting money.

exercises.question: The ____ of this detector is to locate underground cables.
exercises.hint: What it is designed to do.
exercises.explanation: Function describes the purpose of a product.

exercises.question: Since it's ____ to be used in noisy environments, the earphone is an important ____.
exercises.explanation: Products are designed for specific contexts and have specific features.

exercises.question: Are these already on the market - are they ____ products?
exercises.explanation: Existing products are those already on the market.

exercises.question: Or are we talking about ____ products that are still under development?
exercises.explanation: Proposed products are those in the design or development phase.

lessons.title: Design calculations
lessons.theory:
Engineers provide technical requirements in **specifications**. They must **determine** (identify) and **quantify** (calculate) the **loads** (forces) that components will carry. 

Calculations are usually based on a **worst-case scenario** (the maximum possible load). After quantifying these loads, engineers apply a **factor of safety** – an extra margin to ensure the component is strong enough.

**Sizing** components means calculating their required dimensions. If an engineer adds excessive safety margins, they **overdesign** the component. This is sometimes called a **belt and braces** approach.

exercises.question: The types of loads that will be encountered must be ____.
exercises.explanation: Engineers must determine what loads a structure will face.

exercises.question: Maximum loads are based on predicted ____.
exercises.explanation: Worst-case scenarios account for the maximum possible force.

exercises.question: On top of maximum loads, additional safety margins are ____.
exercises.explanation: Safety margins are factored in to ensure reliability.

exercises.question: For cost reasons, components shouldn't be ____.
exercises.explanation: Overdesigning increases costs unnecessarily.

exercises.question: The practice of overdesigning components can be described as the ____ approach.
exercises.explanation: Belt and braces is an idiom for extreme caution.

exercises.question: ____ components means calculating their dimensions.
exercises.explanation: Sizing is the calculation of required dimensions.

lessons.title: Professional terminology
lessons.theory: In engineering, it is important to use the correct terminology when discussing safety and costs. For example, instead of saying 'make provision for', we say **allow for**. Instead of 'calculate an amount', we use **quantify**.

lessons.title: Linear dimensions
lessons.theory:
Engineers use specific terms for linear dimensions:

* **Overall length**: Total measurement from front to rear (along a horizontal plane).
* **Wingspan**: Total distance spanned by both wings.
* **Overall height**: How tall an object is from the ground to the top (measured vertically).
* **Width**: Measurement from side to side.
* **Thickness**: The external or internal dimension of a wall or component.
* **Span**: The distance between supports (e.g., in a bridge).

**Planes** are imaginary surfaces shown as lines on drawings. They **strike** (touch) the faces (edges or surfaces) of components.

exercises.explanation: Overall length is the total measurement from front to rear.

exercises.question: Millau Viaduct (2) Maximum ____ between supports: 342m
exercises.explanation: A span is the distance between supports of a bridge.

exercises.explanation: Width is the horizontal measurement across the deck.

exercises.explanation: Thickness refers to the dimension of the wall or component.

lessons.title: Level and plumb
lessons.theory:
Measurements are taken along horizontal or vertical planes.

* **Level**: A surface that is both horizontal and flat (smooth).
* **Flat**: A surface that is smooth, but not necessarily horizontal (it could be vertical or **inclined**).
* **Plumb**: Faces that are perfectly vertical (like the walls of a building).
* **Out of plumb**: Structures that are slightly inclined from the vertical.

exercises.explanation: False - The greatest thickness is its external thickness at its base.

lessons.title: Power lines and insulators
lessons.theory: On extra-high voltage (EHV) power lines, cables (conductors) span between pylons. They are suspended by rods called **insulators**. On straight sections, insulators hang vertically (**plumb**). At turns, they may be pulled **out of plumb**.

exercises.explanation: Plumb means perfectly vertical.

exercises.question: In this situation, the insulators are inclined from the vertical plane...
exercises.explanation: Inclined means sloping at an angle.

exercises.question: ...as they are pulled out of plumb by the conductors.
exercises.explanation: Out of plumb means not perfectly vertical.

exercises.question: The length of insulators therefore varies, depending on the voltage.
exercises.explanation: Length is the dimension that varies for insulators.

exercises.question: Conductors must be located at a greater minimum height above the ground.
exercises.explanation: Height is the vertical distance above ground level.

lessons.title: Centrelines and offsets
lessons.theory:
To locate points on components, engineers use **centrelines (CL)** – lines through the centre of holes or objects. Distances between centrelines are called **centre-to-centre (c/c)** dimensions. 

Measurements are often **offset** from a centreline, meaning they are at a certain distance from it. Offsets are measured at a **right-angle** (90 degrees) to the centreline.

exercises.explanation: Dimensions between centres are described as 'at X mm centres'.

exercises.explanation: The centreline is the line through the middle of an object.

exercises.question: Replace 'located away from': How far is the widest point ____ the centreline?
exercises.explanation: Offset is the distance from a reference line at a right-angle.

exercises.question: Replace 'at 90 degrees to': Are the adjacent lengths ____ each other?
exercises.explanation: Right-angle means 90 degrees.

exercises.question: Replace 'establish the position': These dimensions allow you to ____ the hole.
exercises.explanation: To locate means to find or mark the position of something.

lessons.title: Grids and setting out
lessons.theory:
In large designs, **grids** are used for horizontal positioning. **Gridlines** are numbered or lettered. Parallel gridlines are regular distances apart. **Perpendicular** lines run at right-angles to each other. 

Gridlines **intersect** (cross) at the centres of columns. Site engineers **set out** (mark the position) of structures by **squaring off** gridlines – marking lines at right-angles using a **theodolite** (an optical device for measuring angles). To **double-check**, diagonal measurements are used.

exercises.explanation: Gridlines are used for reference on large sites.

exercises.question: The positions were marked accurately - they were ____ by our site engineer.
exercises.explanation: Setting out is the process of marking positions on the ground.

exercises.explanation: Perpendicular lines are at 90 degrees to each other.

exercises.question: We'll use the theodolite to ____ the gridline and mark a 90-degree offset.
exercises.explanation: Squaring off means marking a line at a right-angle to another.

lessons.title: Accuracy and checks
lessons.theory: To prevent mistakes, always use a steel tape measure (it does not stretch). Check that both diagonals of a rectangle are equal to ensure corners are right-angles. Measure in two directions to **double-check**.

lessons.title: Key dimensions of circles
lessons.theory:
The geometry of circles is essential in engineering. Key terms include:

* **Circumference**: The outside edge of a circle.
* **Radius**: The distance from the centre to any point on the circumference. If it doesn't change, it is a **constant radius**.
* **Diameter**: The distance across a circle through the centre (2 x radius).
* **Arc**: A part of the circumference (a curved line).
* **Chord**: A straight line between two points on a circle.
* **Concentric circles**: Circles with different diameters that share the same centre.

When a circular object like a tyre is compressed, it **deforms** (changes shape), changing an **arc** into a **chord**.

exercises.explanation: A circle is circular in shape.

exercises.question: Distance from centre to edge of tyre = ____.

exercises.explanation: Diameter is twice the radius.

exercises.question: The tyre has a ____ radius.
exercises.explanation: Constant means staying the same.

exercises.question: A part of a circle is an ____.

exercises.question: When compressed, the tyre becomes ____.
exercises.explanation: Deformation is a change in the original shape.

exercises.question: The edge changes from a ____ line to a straight line.
exercises.explanation: Arcs are curved lines.

exercises.question: A straight line between two points on a circle is a ____.
exercises.explanation: A chord connects two points on the circumference with a straight line.

lessons.title: Pipe dimensions
lessons.theory:
Specific terms are used for pipes:

* **Inside Diameter (ID)** or **Bore**: The internal width.
* **Outside Diameter (OD)**: The external width.
* **Crown**: The top of the outside of a horizontal pipe.
* **Invert**: The bottom of the inside of a horizontal pipe.

exercises.explanation: The crown is the uppermost point of a pipe.

exercises.question: The lowest point of the inside of a horizontal pipe is the ____.
exercises.explanation: The invert is the lowest internal point.

exercises.question: The maximum overall external width of a pipe is the ____.
exercises.explanation: Outside diameter (OD) measures the total width.

exercises.question: The maximum internal width between the pipe walls is the ____.
exercises.explanation: Inside diameter (ID) or bore measures the space inside.

lessons.title: Correcting circle terminology
lessons.theory: It is important not to confuse radius, diameter, circumference, and arc. For example, the distance traveled by a wheel in one turn is the **circumference**, not the radius.

exercises.question: The edges of the road follow ____ (not chords) of a circle.

lessons.title: Precision and tolerance
lessons.theory:
All production processes are **imprecise** to some extent. The sizes of components will **vary** (differ). They will not be 100% **accurate** (exact).

Engineers specify **tolerances** – the acceptable **range** of sizes or allowed **variation**. This is often given as a **deviation** (difference) from a precise size (e.g., ±0.05 mm). 

* **Within tolerance**: A size that is **permissible** (allowed).
* **Outside tolerance**: A size that is not allowed.
* **Tight tolerance** (or **close tolerance**): A very small permissible deviation.
* **Loose tolerance**: A large permissible deviation.

exercises.question: Little deviation allowed: ____
exercises.explanation: Tight tolerance requires high precision.

exercises.question: Large deviation allowed: ____
exercises.explanation: Loose tolerance is easier to achieve.

lessons.title: Fit and mechanical play
lessons.theory:
When components go together, their sizes must match. 

* **Clearance fit**: Leaves **clearance** (a gap) so parts can move or turn freely. 
* **Play**: The amount of movement allowed. Too much play is bad; **insufficient clearance** causes parts to **bind** (not move).
* **Interference fit**: A very tight fit where parts don't move. Often achieved by heating (to **expand**) or cooling (to **contract**) parts before assembly.

lessons.title: Engine blueprinting
lessons.theory: Engine blueprinting involves building an engine to extremely precise specifications by matching parts that are within a specific range of the overall tolerance.

lessons.title: Decimals and fractions
lessons.theory:
In engineering, numbers are expressed as **decimals** (e.g., 0.04) or **fractions** (e.g., 1/100). 

* **Whole numbers**: Numbers like 1, 2, 3 (not decimals).
* **Rounding**: Decimals are often **rounded up** or **rounded down** to a certain number of **decimal places**.
* **Rounding error**: A small error caused by rounding that can add up in calculations.
* **Negligible**: A difference so small it doesn't matter.

exercises.explanation: Decimals are read digit by digit after the point.

exercises.question: Write 1/1000 in words: ____ of an inch.
exercises.explanation: 1/1000 is one thousandth.

exercises.question: The number 0 is called ____ or ____.
exercises.explanation: Both zero and nought are used in English.

exercises.question: 0.25 is a decimal; 1/4 is a ____.
exercises.explanation: Fractions represent parts of a whole using a numerator and denominator.

exercises.question: 0.6368 ≈ 0.637. The number is ____ to three ____.
exercises.explanation: Rounding up increases the last digit.

exercises.question: An error of 0.00001% is ____.
exercises.hint: So small it can be ignored.
exercises.explanation: Negligible means too small to be important.

lessons.title: Basic operations
lessons.theory:
Standard terms for calculations include:

* **Plus** / **Sum**: Addition (+).
* **Minus** / **Less** / **Subtract**: Subtraction (-).
* **Times** / **Multiplied by**: Multiplication (x).
* **Divided by**: Division (÷).
* **Squared**: Raised to the power of 2 (e.g., 3²).
* **Square root**: The value that, when squared, gives the number (e.g., √9).

exercises.question: 14 + 8 = 22. Fourteen ____ eight equals twenty-two.
exercises.explanation: Plus is used for addition.

exercises.question: 100 x 20 = 2,000. One hundred ____ twenty is two thousand.
exercises.explanation: Times is a common word for multiplication.

exercises.question: 7 x 11 = 77. Seven ____ by eleven equals seventy-seven.
exercises.explanation: Multiplied by is the formal term.

exercises.question: 400 ÷ 8 = 50. Four hundred ____ by eight equals fifty.
exercises.explanation: Divided by is used for division.

exercises.question: The ____ of 95 and 2 is 97.
exercises.explanation: Sum is the result of addition.

exercises.question: The ____ of 8 is 64.
exercises.explanation: The square of a number is that number times itself.

exercises.question: If you ____ 30 from 50, it equals 20.
exercises.explanation: Subtract means to take away.

exercises.question: The ____ of 100 is 10.
exercises.explanation: Square root is the inverse of squaring.

exercises.question: 11 ____ is 121.
exercises.explanation: Squared means raised to the power of 2.
Minus is used for subtraction.

lessons.title: Geometry calculations
lessons.theory:
Applying math to geometry:

* **Sum of angles**: 180° in a triangle.
* **Area of a circle**: πr² (Pi times radius squared).
* **Area of a triangle**: (Base x Height) / 2.

exercises.question: The ____ of the three angles in a triangle equals 180 degrees.
exercises.explanation: The sum of angles in any triangle is always 180 degrees.

exercises.question: Area of a circle = the ____ of its radius ____ 3.14.
exercises.explanation: Area = πr².

exercises.question: Area of right-angle triangle = (side A ____ side B) ____ two.
exercises.explanation: Triangle area is half the product of base and height.

exercises.question: Length of side of square = ____ of the square's area.
exercises.explanation: Side = √Area.

exercises.question: If all angles are 60°, the lengths of sides are ____.
exercises.explanation: Equilateral triangles have equal sides and 60° angles.

lessons.title: Area and surface area
lessons.theory:
In engineering, different types of area are important:

* **Cross-sectional area**: The area of a shape if it were cut through. (e.g., area of a wire's conductor = πr²).
* **Surface area**: The total amount of surface exposed to the air or other surroundings (important for cooling).

Units for area include **square millimetres (mm²)** and **square metres (m²)**.

exercises.question: A calculation of πr² for a wire gives its ____.
exercises.explanation: Cross-sectional area is the area of a plane through a component.

exercises.question: The total area to be painted is the ____.
exercises.explanation: Surface area is the total outside area.

exercises.question: Unit: m² = ____.
exercises.explanation: m² is the abbreviation for square metres.

lessons.title: Mass, volume and density
lessons.theory:
These terms have specific meanings in physics and engineering:

* **Mass**: How much matter is in an object (measured in kilograms). It remains constant anywhere in the universe.
* **Volume**: The amount of space an object occupies (measured in **cubic metres (m³)**).
* **Density**: Mass per unit of volume (measured in **kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³)**).
* **Weight**: The force exerted on mass by **gravity** (the pull of the earth).

**Mass = Volume x Density**

exercises.question: Unit: kg/m³ = ____.
exercises.explanation: kg/m³ is the unit for density.

exercises.question: Unit: m³ = ____.
exercises.explanation: m³ is the abbreviation for cubic metres.

exercises.question: Mild steel has a ____ of 7,850 kg/m³.
exercises.explanation: Density is a material property.

exercises.question: The amount of space occupied (0.006 m³) is the ____.
exercises.explanation: Volume is the space inside a 3D object.

exercises.question: Volume x Density (47.3 kg) gives the ____.
exercises.explanation: Mass is calculated from volume and density.

lessons.title: Satellite design challenges
lessons.theory: Designing satellites requires managing mass for launch (against gravity) and area for solar power in space.

exercises.question: Every ____ metre of volume within the rocket is expensive.
exercises.explanation: Volume is measured in cubic units.

exercises.question: Each extra gram of ____ added increases the fuel needed.
exercises.explanation: Mass must be minimized for launch.

exercises.question: Propelling it upwards against the pull of ____.
exercises.explanation: Gravity is the force that pulls objects down.

exercises.question: Extra fuel will ____ a little more.
exercises.explanation: Weight is the force caused by gravity.

exercises.question: The satellite must be as ____ as possible.
exercises.explanation: Lightweight materials are crucial for space flight.

exercises.question: In orbit, the satellite is now ____.
exercises.explanation: Objects in orbit experience weightlessness.

exercises.question: Solar panels cover an area of several ____ metres.
exercises.explanation: Area is measured in square units.

lessons.title: Supply, demand and capacity
lessons.theory:
In engineering, managing resource usage involves understanding several key terms:

* **Consumption**: The amount of a resource (like electricity or fuel) being used. The **rate of consumption** is the amount used at a particular moment.
* **Demand**: The requirement for a resource. It often **fluctuates** (rises and falls), reaching a **peak** at certain times.
* **Capacity**: The maximum amount a system can supply or hold. If a system is running at its maximum capability, it is running **to capacity**.
* **Spare capacity**: The difference between the maximum capacity and the current demand.

exercises.question: Fuel (1) ____ for this engine is about 1.2 litres per hour.
exercises.explanation: Consumption rate describes how much fuel is used over time.

exercises.question: Sometimes it will (2) ____ a bit more, sometimes a bit less.
exercises.explanation: To consume is the action of using a resource.

exercises.question: 1.2 is an (3) ____ figure, not always the exact rate.
exercises.explanation: Averages provide a general idea despite fluctuations.

exercises.question: The (4) ____ of a work shift is 8 hours.
exercises.explanation: Duration is the length of time an activity lasts.

exercises.question: It won't be 8 hours of (5) ____ running.
exercises.explanation: Constant running means no stops or changes in rate.

exercises.question: Running at a (6) ____ of 1.2 litres per hour gives 9.6 litres of (7) ____ consumption.
exercises.hint: Amount per hour and total combined.
exercises.explanation: Cumulative consumption is the total amount used over a period.

exercises.question: The (8) ____ of the fuel tank needs to be 10 litres minimum.
exercises.explanation: Capacity is the maximum volume a container can hold.

exercises.question: Water consumption fluctuated between (9) ____ and (10) ____ litres per second.
exercises.hint: Look at the lowest and highest points on the graph.
exercises.explanation: The graph shows a minimum of 4 and a peak of 8.

exercises.question: Averaged out over the period shown, consumption was roughly (11) ____ litres per second.
exercises.explanation: The average of 4 and 8 is 6.

exercises.question: Consumption peaked at a rate of (12) ____ litres per second.
exercises.explanation: Peak consumption is the maximum rate reached.

exercises.question: If the process ran to capacity, it could use water at (13) ____ l/s.
exercises.explanation: The max capacity of the supply is 10 l/s.

exercises.question: When consumption peaked, the process had spare capacity of (14) ____ l/s.
exercises.explanation: 10 (capacity) - 8 (peak) = 2 (spare capacity).

lessons.title: Input, output and efficiency
lessons.theory:
Systems transform energy or materials:

* **Input**: The amount put into a system.
* **Output**: The amount produced or used by consumers.
* **Loss**: Energy or material wasted during the process (e.g., as heat).
* **Gain**: An increase in efficiency or quantity.
* **Efficiency**: The ratio of useful output to total input.

exercises.question: A lot of heat is generated; all of that (1) ____ is recycled.
exercises.hint: Is it what goes in or what comes out?
exercises.explanation: Generated heat is an output of the process.

exercises.question: It provides a (2) ____ of heat for the next stage.
exercises.hint: Does it require heat or provide it?
exercises.explanation: Recycled heat acts as a supply for other stages.

exercises.question: This makes it an (3) ____ system.
exercises.explanation: Recycling waste energy increases efficiency.

exercises.question: Sometimes there is (4) ____ heat, and it can't all be recycled.
exercises.explanation: Surplus means there is extra that isn't needed.

exercises.question: At other times there isn't enough to keep up with (5) ____ demand.
exercises.explanation: Peak demand is the maximum requirement.

exercises.question: There's a net (6) ____ in total mass because water is absorbed.
exercises.hint: Does total mass increase or decrease?
exercises.explanation: A gain means the final mass is greater than the initial.

lessons.title: Metals and non-metals
lessons.theory:
Engineering materials are classified into:

* **Metals**: Examples include iron (Fe), copper (Cu), and aluminium (Al).
* **Non-metals**: Examples include carbon (C) and silicon (Si).
* **Ferrous metals**: Metals that contain iron (e.g., steel).
* **Non-ferrous metals**: Metals that do not contain iron (e.g., aluminium, copper).

exercises.question: Carbon (C) is a (1) ____.
exercises.explanation: Carbon is a primary non-metallic element.

exercises.question: Copper (Cu) is a (2) ____ metal.
exercises.explanation: Non-ferrous metals lack iron.

exercises.question: Aluminium (Al) is a common (3) ____.
exercises.explanation: Aluminium is a highly common metallic element.

exercises.question: Steel (Fe + C) is a widely used (4) ____ metal.
exercises.explanation: Ferrous metals are iron-based.

exercises.question: Although it is used in steel, carbon is (5) ____.
exercises.explanation: Carbon itself does not have metallic properties.

exercises.question: Aluminium is relatively lightweight for a (6) ____ material.
exercises.explanation: Aluminium is a light metal compared to others.

lessons.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
lessons.theory:
Materials have different chemical compositions:

* **Elements**: Pure materials in their basic form (e.g., iron, carbon).
* **Compounds**: Elements chemically bound by a reaction (e.g., water - H₂O).
* **Mixtures / Alloys**: Elements or compounds mixed together but not chemically bound. **Alloys** are metals mixed with other elements (e.g., steel is an iron-carbon alloy).

exercises.question: The elements in a compound are chemically bound.
exercises.explanation: True - Compounds consist of chemically bound elements.

exercises.question: Alloys are chemical compounds frequently used in engineering.
exercises.hint: Are alloys bound chemically or just mixed?
exercises.explanation: False - Alloys are mixtures, not chemical compounds.

exercises.question: Alloys can contain both metallic and non-metallic constituents.
exercises.explanation: True - Steel is an alloy of iron (metal) and carbon (non-metal).

exercises.question: In an alloy, an alloying metal is the biggest constituent.
exercises.explanation: False - The base metal is the biggest constituent; alloying metals are added in smaller amounts.

exercises.question: Steel is a metallic element.
exercises.hint: Is it pure or a mixture?
exercises.explanation: False - Steel is an alloy (mixture), not an element.

lessons.title: Composite materials
lessons.theory:
Composites consist of a **matrix** and **reinforcement**:

* **Matrix**: The surrounding material (e.g., plastic).
* **Reinforcement**: The structural network inside (e.g., glass fibres).
* **Examples**: 
    * Bricks (mud matrix, straw reinforcement).
    * Fibreglass / GRP (plastic matrix, glass fibre reinforcement).
    * Reinforced concrete (concrete matrix, steel reinforcement).

exercises.question: (1) ____ concrete is widely used. Steel bars (2) ____ the structure.
exercises.explanation: Reinforced (adj) and reinforce (verb) describe the structural strengthening.

exercises.question: The concrete and the steel (3) ____ expand at the same rate.
exercises.explanation: Reinforcement is the noun for the reinforcing material.

exercises.question: Using a (4) ____ material with a different coefficient would not be feasible.
exercises.explanation: Reinforcing (adj) describes the function of the material.

exercises.question: Aluminium-(5) ____ concrete would quickly disintegrate.
exercises.explanation: Reinforced describes the concrete containing reinforcement.

exercises.question: Identify the material category for each item:
exercises.explanation: Elements are pure; compounds are chemically bound; alloys are metallic mixtures; composites combine matrix and reinforcement.

lessons.title: Carbon steels and alloy steels
lessons.theory:
Steel is an alloy of iron (Fe) and carbon (C). It is divided into two main categories:

* **Carbon steels**: Contain only iron and carbon. Grades include **mild steel** (low carbon), **medium carbon steel**, and **high carbon steel**.
* **Alloy steels**: Contain iron, carbon, and alloying metals (e.g., chromium, nickel).
    * **HSLA (High strength low alloy)**: Contains small amounts of alloying metals (less than 2%).
    * **Stainless steel**: Contains chromium (Cr) and nickel (Ni); highly corrosion-resistant.
    * **Tool steel**: Extremely hard; contains tungsten (W) or cobalt (Co). **High-speed steel** is used for drill bits.

exercises.question: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon.
exercises.explanation: True - Steel consists primarily of iron and carbon.

exercises.question: Mild steel is a high carbon steel.
exercises.explanation: False - Mild steel is a low carbon steel (up to 0.3%).

exercises.question: Alloy steels contain carbon.
exercises.explanation: True - All steels contain carbon, even those with other alloying metals.

exercises.question: Chromium and nickel are used as alloying metals in steel.
exercises.explanation: True - Chromium and nickel are frequent alloying elements, especially in stainless steel.

exercises.question: Low alloy steels contain more chromium than iron.
exercises.explanation: False - Low alloy steels are mostly iron (90%+).

exercises.question: Stainless steel is an alloy steel.
exercises.hint: Is it a category or a pure element?
exercises.explanation: True - Stainless steel is a type of alloy steel.

exercises.question: Tungsten is added to steel to make it softer.
exercises.explanation: False - Tungsten is added to increase hardness.

exercises.question: High-speed steel is suitable for cutting tools that get very hot.
exercises.explanation: True - High-speed steel maintains hardness at high temperatures.

lessons.title: Corrosion
lessons.theory:
Corrosion is a chemical reaction between iron and oxygen (O₂) to form **iron oxide** (**rust**).

* **Rusting**: Specifically refers to the corrosion of iron-based metals.
* **Oxidation**: The reaction with oxygen.
* **Passive layer**: Metals like aluminium form a hard oxide layer that prevents further corrosion. Mild steel, however, flakes off, allowing corrosion to continue.

exercises.question: When steel is exposed to air and water, it (1) ____.
exercises.explanation: Steel rusts when exposed to moisture and air.

exercises.question: A brown/red material on the surface of steel is called (2) ____.
exercises.explanation: Rust is the common name for iron oxide.

exercises.question: The strength of steel is reduced if it is (3) ____.
exercises.explanation: Corroded steel loses structural integrity.

exercises.question: The problem with mild (1) ____ is that it (2) ____. Solution is to use a (3) ____ of steel resistant to the (4) ____ process, like (5) ____ steel which contains (6) ____ and nickel.
exercises.explanation: Stainless steel is a corrosion-resistant grade containing chromium.

exercises.question: Weathering steel surface is allowed to go (7) ____. Once a layer of (8) ____ has formed, it stabilizes. It differs from ordinary (9) ____ oxide.
exercises.explanation: Weathering steel uses a stable rust layer for protection.

lessons.title: Common non-ferrous metals
lessons.theory:
Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron:

* **Aluminium**: Lightweight, often alloyed with titanium or copper. **Duralumin** contains aluminium, copper (4.4%) and magnesium (1.5%).
* **Copper**: Excellent electrical conductor, ductile (used for wires and pipes). Alloys: **Brass** (copper + zinc) and **Bronze** (copper + tin + lead).
* **Titanium**: High strength-to-weight ratio; used in aerospace.
* **Precious metals**: High-cost metals. **Silver** is the best electrical conductor. **Gold** is an excellent conductor and highly corrosion-resistant.

exercises.question: Match the metal/alloy with its description:

pairs.right: Aluminium alloy with copper and magnesium
Mixed with tin and lead to make bronze
Mixed with copper to make brass

exercises.explanation: These are key characteristics of non-ferrous metals and their alloys.

exercises.question: Duralumin contains copper (4.4%) and (1) ____ (1.5%).
exercises.explanation: Magnesium is a key alloying element in duralumin.

lessons.title: Plating and anodizing
lessons.theory:
Non-ferrous metals can protect steel from corrosion by **plating** it:

* **Galvanizing**: Coating steel with zinc (hot-dip or electro-galvanized).
* **Electroplating**: Depositing metal via electric current. 
    * The component is the **cathode** (-).
    * The plating metal (e.g. zinc) is the **anode** (+).
    * The bath contains an **electrolyte** liquid.
* **Anodizing**: Protecting aluminium by depositing a hard oxide layer on the component (functioning as the anode).

exercises.question: Check that there is sufficient (1) ____ in the bath to cover the component, ensuring it is (2) ____ over its entire area.
exercises.hint: The liquid and the process result.
exercises.explanation: Electrolyte is the conducting liquid; plating is the process.

exercises.question: The component is connected to the (3) ____ terminal and functions as the (5) ____ during the (4) ____ process.
exercises.explanation: The negative electrode in electroplating is the cathode.

exercises.question: Zinc for (6) ____ is connected to the (7) ____ terminal and functions as the (8) ____.
exercises.explanation: Galvanizing is zinc plating; the positive electrode is the anode.

lessons.title: Natural and synthetic polymers
lessons.theory:
Polymers are compounds made of huge molecules joined in long chains. Each molecule contains many atoms.

* **Natural polymers**: Occur in nature (e.g., rubber from latex in rubber trees).
* **Synthetic polymers**: Manmade materials (e.g., plastics).
* **Molecular structure**: Most compounds have small molecules; polymers have massive chains.

exercises.question: A lot of rubber is made from latex, a (1) ____ polymer which comes from rubber trees.
exercises.explanation: Latex is a biological product, hence natural.

exercises.question: Synthetic rubber is a (2) ____ polymer with similar properties to latex.
exercises.explanation: Synthetic means manmade.

exercises.question: Like rubber, plastics consist of long chains of (3) ____ which form extremely large (4) ____.
exercises.explanation: Atoms join to form molecules; in polymers, these molecules are huge.

lessons.title: Thermoplastics and thermosets
lessons.theory:
Synthetic polymers are divided into:

* **Thermoplastics**: Can be melted and remoulded multiple times (e.g., ABS, PVC, polycarbonate).
* **Thermosetting plastics (Thermosets)**: Set permanently after heating or mixing (**cure**) and cannot be remoulded. If heated again, they burn (e.g., epoxy resins).
* **Elastomers**: Very elastic polymers that can stretch and return to their original length.

exercises.question: The plastic has now fully cooled and set. Any products that fail the tests are melted down and reused.

options.text: The plastic was heated earlier in the process.
The material is a thermosetting plastic.

exercises.explanation: Reusing material by melting it down confirms it is a thermoplastic.

exercises.question:
1. Shorter name for polyvinylchloride: (1) ____
2. Used for forming melted plastic: (2) ____
3. A group of atoms: (3) ____
4. A long chain of atoms: (4) ____
5. To set permanently: (5) ____
6. A very elastic polymer: (6) ____
exercises.explanation: These terms cover the basic properties and processing of polymers.

exercises.question:
7. A plastic that sets permanently: (7) ____
8. A natural polymer: (8) ____
9. A very strong thermoset resin: (9) ____
10. Not natural: (10) ____
11. Particles that form molecules: (11) ____
12. Another word for 'not natural': (12) ____
13. Material used to make rubber: (13) ____
exercises.explanation: Synthetic, manmade, and thermoset are key industrial terms.

lessons.title: Mineral and ceramic materials
lessons.theory:
Materials from the ground:

* **Minerals**: Natural, inorganic materials found in rocks (e.g., iron ore, diamond, silicon).
* **Ceramics**: Inorganic, non-metallic materials formed by heating (e.g., glass, bricks).
* **Vitrified**: Ceramics that have been heated to form a glass-like structure.
* **Firing**: Heating clay in a **kiln** (industrial oven) to make bricks.

exercises.question: Match the mineral/ceramic term with its definition:

pairs.right: Natural inorganic material found in rocks
Very hard material used for cutting/grinding

exercises.explanation: These terms are essential for understanding mineral and ceramic properties.

exercises.question: The clay bricks were (1) ____ in a (2) ____.
exercises.explanation: Firing in a kiln is the standard production method for bricks.

lessons.title: Glass and safety glass
lessons.theory:
Glass manufacturing and types:

* **Float glass**: Flat sheets made by floating molten glass on molten tin.
* **Annealed glass**: Glass cooled slowly; breaks into dangerous shards.
* **Tempered / Toughened glass**: Heated and then cooled to change its structure; shatters into tiny pieces when broken.
* **Laminated glass**: A 'sandwich' of glass and polymer layers; stays **intact** on breaking as pieces are **bonded** to the polymer.

exercises.question: Most flat glass is (1) ____ glass, produced on a bed of molten (2) ____.
exercises.explanation: The float process produces high-quality flat glass.

exercises.question: Which type of glass shatters into tiny pieces?
exercises.explanation: Toughened (tempered) glass is designed to shatter into harmless granules.

exercises.question: Laminated glass stays (3) ____ because the shards are (4) ____ to a thin (5) ____ layer.
exercises.explanation: The polymer interlayer holds the glass pieces together upon impact.

lessons.title: Concrete mix design
lessons.theory:
Concrete is a mixture of **cement**, **fine aggregate** (sand), **coarse aggregate** (gravel), and water. 

* **Set**: When concrete begins to become solid.
* **28-day strength**: The point where concrete reaches its structural strength.
* **Batching**: Measuring precise quantities of ingredients by weight.
* **Water-cement ratio**: The amount of water relative to cement; excess water reduces strength.
* **Additives**: Chemicals like **plasticizers** (to help flow) or **retarders** (to delay setting).

exercises.question:
1. Gravel used in concrete: (1) ____
2. Sand used in concrete: (2) ____
3. Powder that enables concrete to set: (3) ____
4. Mixing concrete accurately: (4) ____
5. Specification of concrete ingredients: (5) ____
exercises.explanation: These terms are fundamental to concrete technology.

exercises.question:
6. Effective structural capability: (6) ____
7. Affects wetness and strength: (7) ____
8. Chemicals put in concrete: (8) ____
9. Allows concrete to stay wet longer: (9) ____
10. Makes drier concrete easier to work with: (10) ____
exercises.explanation: Strength and workability are controlled by ratios and additives.

lessons.title: Reinforced and prestressed concrete
lessons.theory:
Concrete is weak in **tension** (stretching), so steel **reinforcement** bars are added.

* **Formwork** / **Shuttering**: Moulds used to contain wet concrete until it sets.
* **In-situ**: Concrete cast in its final position.
* **Precast**: Concrete elements cast at a factory and then delivered.
* **Prestressing**: Applying tension to reinforcing bars before (**pre-tensioning**) or after (**post-tensioning**) pouring to increase resistance to bending.

exercises.question: Post-tensioning is a type of (1) ____. The bars are (2) ____ inside a plastic tube. They are not (3) ____ at first. After the concrete has (4) ____, the bars are (5) ____.
exercises.explanation: Post-tensioning involves tensioning bars after the concrete sets.

exercises.question: Concrete is weak in which type of force?
exercises.explanation: Concrete has high compressive strength but very low tensile strength.

lessons.title: Categories of wood
lessons.theory:
Wood is divided into two biological categories:

* **Hardwood**: From deciduous trees (e.g., oak).
* **Softwood**: From coniferous trees (e.g., pine).

Engineering formats:

* **Solid wood**: Sawn timber with natural grain and knots.
* **Engineered wood**: Made by bonding layers or particles with resin (e.g., plywood, OSB, glulam).

exercises.question: Match the wood category with its property:

pairs.right: Always made from multiple pieces or particles bonded together
Single pieces of timber that may have knots

exercises.explanation: These distinctions are vital for structural design and material selection.

exercises.question: Coniferous trees provide a source of (1) ____. Hardwood comes from (2) ____ trees.
exercises.explanation: Softwood and hardwood are biological classifications, not necessarily indicators of density.

lessons.title: Structural timber and engineered wood
lessons.theory:
Structural timber is tested to determine its **stress grade**:

* **Rough-sawn**: Surface texture from circular saws.
* **Planed**: Smoothed surface for visibility.
* **Stress-grading**: Mechanical (by machine) or visual (by inspector).
* **Glulams**: Glue-laminated sections used for large structural beams.
* **Plywood**: Layers (**plies**) bonded with grain at 90 degrees.

exercises.question: Timber has a smooth finish after it has been (1) ____. Saw-cut timber is called (2) ____. After testing, it is given a (3) ____.
exercises.explanation: Planing removes the rough surface; grading ensures structural safety.

exercises.question: Sustainable (1) ____ trees provide wood for solid, (2) ____ sections, (3) ____ beams, and (4) ____ plies. Smaller strands make (5) ____, while particles make (6) ____ board and (7) ____.
exercises.explanation: Wood utilization ranges from high-grade structural beams to recycled particle boards.

lessons.title: Tensile strength and deformation
lessons.theory:
Materials react to forces:

* **Tension**: Stretching forces. Causes **extension** or **elongation**.
* **Compression**: Crushing forces.
* **Deformation**: Change in shape due to force.
* **Tensile strength**: Ability to resist tension.
* **Compressive strength**: Ability to resist compression.

exercises.question:
1. Increase in length: (1) ____
2. Ability to resist stretching: (2) ____
3. Ability to resist crushing: (3) ____
4. Ability to return to shape: (4) ____
5. Easy to fracture: (5) ____
6. Can be drawn into wires: (6) ____
exercises.explanation: These properties define how materials behave under mechanical stress.

lessons.title: Elastic and plastic deformation
lessons.theory:
Materials go through stages of deformation:

* **Proportional extension**: Length increases linearly with tension.
* **Elastic limit**: The point beyond which a material will not return to its original shape.
* **Yield point**: The point where the material begins to flow and extend significantly without added force.
* **UTS (Ultimate Tensile Strength)**: The maximum tension a material can withstand before breaking.

exercises.question:
1. Length increases linearly with tension: (1) ____
2. Point of no return for shape: (2) ____
3. Permanent deformation: (3) ____
4. Material gives way and flows: (4) ____
5. Maximum tensile capability: (5) ____
exercises.explanation: The transition from elastic to plastic behavior is critical in engineering design.

exercises.question: What happens when a ductile material reaches its UTS?

options.text: It begins to neck and then fractures

exercises.explanation: After UTS, a material necks (gets thinner) and eventually fractures.

lessons.title: Hardness, fatigue and creep
lessons.theory:
Durability depends on several factors:

* **Indentation hardness**: Resistance to impacts (preventing dents).
* **Scratch hardness**: Resistance to surface scratches; related to **abrasion resistance**.
* **Fatigue**: Caused by **cyclic loads** (varying forces). Results in **micro-cracking**.
* **Fracture toughness**: Measure of how easily existing cracks open up.
* **Creep**: Permanent deformation due to sustained loads over time, worsened by heat.

exercises.question: The guards must have high (1) ____ hardness to protect from impacts. Wiping away metal fragments causes (2) ____, so they need (3) ____ hardness for (4) ____.
exercises.explanation: Indentation resists impact; scratch/abrasion resists surface wear.

exercises.question:
1. Forces that continually vary: (1) ____
2. Problem caused by cyclic loads: (2) ____
3. Formation of tiny cracks: (3) ____
4. Measure of how easily cracks open: (4) ____
5. Permanent deformation due to sustained loads: (5) ____
exercises.explanation: Fatigue and creep are common causes of structural failure over time.

lessons.title: Thermal properties
lessons.theory:
How materials handle heat:

* **Thermal conductivity**: Ability to **conduct** (transmit) heat.
* **Thermal conductor**: Material with high conductivity (e.g., copper).
* **Thermal insulator**: Material with poor conductivity (e.g., polystyrene).
* **Expansion** / **Contraction**: Increase/decrease in size due to temperature changes.
* **Coefficient of thermal expansion**: Change in size per degree of temperature change.

exercises.question:
1. Ability to transmit heat: (1) ____
2. Material that transmits heat well: (2) ____
3. Material that is a poor conductor: (3) ____
4. Increase in size due to heat: (4) ____
5. Decrease in size due to cooling: (5) ____
exercises.explanation: Thermal management is crucial in engineering to prevent overheating or structural failure due to expansion.

units.title: Unit 20: Forming, working and heat-treating metal

lessons.title: Casting, sintering and extruding
lessons.theory:
Metal forming processes:

* **Casting**: Pouring molten metal into a mould (**die**).
* **Sintering**: Compressing metal powder in a die and heating it (without melting) until particles join.
* **Extrusion**: Forcing molten metal through a shaping die to form long lengths (bars, tubes).

exercises.question: Which process uses metal powder instead of molten metal?
exercises.explanation: Sintering joins powder particles through heat and pressure without melting.

exercises.question: In casting and extrusion, the metal must be (1) ____. All three processes use a (2) ____ to shape the metal.
exercises.explanation: Molten metal is required for flow; a die provides the shape.

lessons.title: Working and heat-treating
lessons.theory:
Shaping and improving metal properties:

* **Forging** / **Working**: Shaping metal by hammering or rolling (**hot** or **cold**).
* **Work hardening**: Increased hardness due to cold working.
* **Shot-peening**: Firing metal balls at a surface to harden it.
* **Heat treatments**:
    * **Annealing**: Heating and slow cooling (softens, increases elasticity).
    * **Quencing**: Rapid cooling (hardens, increases brittleness).
    * **Tempering**: Heating and holding (balances hardness and elasticity).
    * **Precipitation hardening** (**age hardening**): Extended tempering for maximum hardness.
    * **Case hardening**: Hardening only the surface using specific gases.

exercises.question: Decide if these sentences are true or false:

options.text: Metal must always be heated before it can be forged.
Forging increases the hardness of metal (work hardening).
Shot-peening is a hot forging technique.
Metal can be rolled cold or hot.

exercises.explanation: Cold working is common; shot-peening is always cold.

exercises.question: Match the heat treatment with its result:

pairs.right: Makes metal softer and more elastic
Makes metal harder but more brittle
Also called age hardening; very hard

exercises.explanation: Different cooling rates and chemical environments produce different metallic properties.

lessons.title: Raw materials and basic blocks
lessons.theory:
Raw materials often require processing before use (e.g., melting/casting). Common formats:

* **Powder**: Very fine particles (e.g., cement).
* **Pellets**: Standard pea-to-egg sized pieces (e.g., plastic).
* **Fibres**: Hair-like lengths (e.g., glass fibres).
* **Ingots**: Large blocks of metal produced at foundries.
* **Blooms**: Very large steel ingots.
* **Billets**: Smaller blocks of steel.

exercises.question: Decide if these sentences are true or false:

options.text: Raw materials are often intended to be melted or mixed.
Powder particles are larger than pellets.
A steel bloom is a type of ingot.
Steel blooms can be cut into smaller pieces called billets.

exercises.hint: Size and scale of raw blocks.
exercises.explanation: Blooms are large; billets are small; powder is the finest.

lessons.title: Processed formats
lessons.theory:
Materials are supplied in ready-to-use formats:

* **Bars**: Solid long lengths (round/rod, square, flat).
* **Sheets**: Flat, wide, thin (<3mm for steel). Wood sheets are **boards**; metal sheets come in **coils**.
* **Plates**: Flat, wide, thick (>3mm for steel).
* **Sections**: Structural shapes (e.g., I-sections).
* **Tubes**: Hollow lengths. **Pipes** carry liquid/gas.
* **Wires**: Single strands of metal. Combined wires form a **cable**.

exercises.question:
1. A long, thin circular section of any material: (1) ____
2. Thin metal supplied in a roll: (2) ____
3. Thick, flat piece of metal: (3) ____
4. Hollow length for carrying liquid: (4) ____
5. Group of insulated conductors: (5) ____
exercises.explanation: Precise names for formats are essential for procurement and design specifications.

exercises.question: Metal sheets of wood are called (1) ____. Single strands of metal are (2) ____, while grouped strands are (3) ____ wires.
exercises.explanation: Terminological nuances distinguish between wood boards and metal sheets/wires.

lessons.title: Machining and CNC
lessons.theory:
Machining involves cutting and shaping material (**workpieces**) into components.

* **Machine tools**: Tools used for cutting (e.g., drill bits).
* **Swarf / Chips**: Waste metal produced.
* **Cutting fluid / Coolant**: Liquid pumped onto the workpiece to keep it cool.
* **CNC (Computer Numerical Control)**: Computers guiding the machining process.
* **CAD/CAM**: Software for design and direct transfer to CNC.

exercises.question: Match the machining term with its role:
exercises.explanation: These terms are standard in industrial manufacturing environments.

lessons.title: Cutting tools and techniques
lessons.theory:
Common machining techniques:

* **Milling**: Rotating cutters move over a fixed workpiece.
* **Turning**: Workpiece rotates on a **lathe**; a fixed tool cuts it.
* **Sawing**: Cutting with a blade (e.g., **hacksaw**, **band saw**). The gap left is the **kerf**.
* **Drilling**: Rotating a **drill bit** to make holes. **Boring** enlarges existing holes.
* **Grinding**: Surface material removal using **abrasive wheels**.

exercises.question:
1. A tool for making holes: (1) ____ bit
2. A hollow saw for cutting out cores: (2) ____
3. A tool for cutting metal by hand: (3) ____
4. A rotating wheel with a rough surface: (4) ____ wheel
5. The gap left by a saw blade: (5) ____
exercises.explanation: Each tool is specialized for a particular material and desired finish.

exercises.question:
1. Lathes are used to (1) ____ workpieces. 
2. (2) ____ involves removing material across a surface. 
3. Toothed cutting wheels are used to (3) ____ workpieces. 
4. Sawing blades remove material to form a (4) ____.
exercises.explanation: The choice of process depends on the geometry of the required part.

lessons.title: Guillotining and punching
lessons.theory:
Cutting thin materials using pressure (**shear force**):

* **Guillotining**: Making long, straight cuts with a blade.
* **Punching**: Using a **die** to make small, shaped cuts.
* **Blanking**: Producing small, shaped workpieces (**blanks**) from a sheet.
* **Piercing**: Making holes in a sheet where the sheet is the final product.

exercises.question: Match the shearing process with its description:

pairs.left: Making holes in a finished sheet
Using a shaped die to shear metal

exercises.explanation: Shearing is a non-chip-forming process used primarily for sheet metal.

lessons.title: High-temperature and waterjet cutting
lessons.theory:
Advanced cutting technologies:

* **Flame-cutting**: Using **oxyacetylene** (oxygen + acetylene) to melt steel.
* **EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining)**: Also called **spark erosion**; using an **electric arc** to melt metal ahead of a wire.
* **Plasma cutting**: Using **ionized** gas (plasma) at extremely high temperatures.
* **Laser cutting**: Using concentrated light to melt material.
* **UHP Waterjet**: Using extremely high-pressure water. Advantage: no **HAZ** (heat-affected zone) and no **secondary operations** needed.

exercises.question: Flame-cutting uses a mixture of (1) ____ and (2) ____ called (3) ____. UHP (4) ____ cutting has high (5) ____, so no (6) ____ operations are needed to smooth edges.
exercises.explanation: Waterjets are ideal for materials sensitive to heat, as they avoid creating a HAZ.

exercises.question:
1. What EDM stands for: (1) ____
2. Alternative name for EDM: (2) ____ erosion
3. Tool used in flame and plasma cutting: (3) ____
4. Heat source in EDM: (4) ____
5. Gas that has been ionized: (5) ____
6. Concentrated light beam: (6) ____
7. Area changed by heat: (7) ____
exercises.explanation: These advanced techniques allow for precise cutting of hard or complex materials.

lessons.title: Attaching and supporting
lessons.theory:
Components in assemblies are connected in various ways:

* **Supported**: Preventing downward movement.
* **Anchored**: Holding in position to stop sliding or lifting.
* **Embedded**: Surrounded and held (e.g., bolts in concrete).
* **Joint / Connection**: The point where components meet.
* **Fastened together / Fixed**: Securely joined using fasteners.

exercises.question: A bridge's cables are (1) ____ by towers and (2) ____ at each end by concrete blocks deeply (3) ____ in the ground. The smaller cables are (4) ____ to the main cable by a saddle, which is fixed (5) ____ by bolts.
exercises.explanation: Proper support and anchoring are essential for large-scale engineering structures like bridges.

lessons.title: Fitting and adjustment
lessons.theory:
Ensuring components fit properly:

* **Play**: The amount of free movement allowed in a joint.
* **Adjusted**: Moved as required for alignment.
* **Slot through**: Passing a component through a hole.
* **Fit together**: Correct matching of parts.
* **Sealed**: Protected against environmental factors (e.g., rainwater).

exercises.question: Match the technical issue with its consequence:

pairs.right: They won't slot through the holes
There is too much play even when tightened

pairs.left: Holes do not line up exactly
pairs.right: The parts won't fit together properly
The assembly is not protected against corrosion

exercises.explanation: Precision in manufacturing and assembly prevents structural failure and environmental damage.

lessons.title: Bolts and nuts
lessons.theory:
Common fasteners include bolts and nuts:

* **Threaded shaft** (**shank**): The part of the bolt with grooves.
* **Nut**: Screwed onto the bolt by a turning motion (usually clockwise).
* **Socket head**: A hexagonal hole in the bolt head for a **hex key** (**Allen key**).
* **Spanner** / **Wrench**: Tools used to turn hexagonal heads.

exercises.question: Which of these sentences is correct?

options.text: Wrenches are a type of fastener.
Nuts are usually screwed on by turning them clockwise.
The threaded part of a bolt is the head.
Allen keys fit around the outside of a bolt head.

exercises.explanation: Nuts and bolts are fasteners; wrenches and Allen keys are tools used to tighten them.

lessons.title: Torque and washers
lessons.theory:
Managing force in joints:

* **Torque**: The turning force applied to a bolt.
* **Preload** (**clamp load**): The pressing force that holds components together.
* **Work loose**: When a joint becomes loose over time due to vibration.
* **Washers**:
    * **Plain washers**: Spread the load over a wider area.
    * **Spring washers**: Compressed to allow preload adjustment or absorb shocks.

exercises.question: It is essential to (1) ____ bolts correctly to ensure the right amount of (2) ____. If you (3) ____ a bolt, the (4) ____ in the shank might cause it to fail. Excess (5) ____ can damage the threads, causing the nut to slip and the joint to (6) ____ over time.
exercises.explanation: Correct torque prevents both loosening and structural damage to the fastener.

exercises.question: Match the washer type to its purpose:

pairs.right: Spread the load across the surface

exercises.explanation: Washers protect the surface and maintain the integrity of the bolted joint.

lessons.title: Screws and anchors
lessons.theory:
Screws and wall fixings:

* **Self-tapping screws**: Cut their own holes without predrilling.
* **Machine screws**: Small-diameter bolts used with nuts or threaded holes.
* **Set screws** (**grub screws**): Hold components in place by pressure (e.g., a wheel on a shaft).
* **Screw anchors** (**wall plugs**): Expand in a hole to resist **pullout forces**.
* **Chemical anchors**: Studs set in a hole using **epoxy resin**.

exercises.question: Match the screw type with its feature:

pairs.right: Does not require a predrilled hole
Applies pressure at its end to hold a part
Has a straight groove for the screwdriver

exercises.explanation: The type of screw chosen depends on the material and the force it must withstand.

exercises.question: To fix an object to a wall, you insert a (1) ____ into a hole. As you drive in the (2) ____, the plug (3) ____, increasing friction to resist (4) ____ force. For very high loads, a (5) ____ can be (6) ____ using epoxy resin.
exercises.explanation: Anchors rely on friction or chemical bonding to stay secure in masonry.

lessons.title: Rivets
lessons.theory:
Permanent fasteners:

* **Solid rivets**: Consist of a shaft with a **factory head**. A tool deforms the other end to form a **shop head**.
* **Blind rivets** (**pop rivets**): Hollow tubes fitted using a **rivet gun** from one side only.
* **Rivet gun**: The tool used to install blind rivets.

exercises.question: Which statement about rivets is TRUE?

options.text: Solid rivets have a shop head and a factory head.
Blind rivets are stronger than solid rivets.
A rivet gun is used for solid rivets.

exercises.explanation: Rivets are permanent fasteners; solid ones are standard in aircraft construction.

lessons.title: Welding principles
lessons.theory:
Joining by melting and fusion:

* **Fusion**: Material from each component is mixed in the **weld pool**.
* **Base metal**: The metal the components are made of.
* **Filler**: New material added to the joint.
* **Heat-affected zone (HAZ)**: Material close to the weld modified by heat.
* **Residual stress**: Tension 'trapped' around the joint after cooling.

exercises.question: In welding, the edges of the components become (1) ____ and (2) ____ occurs. One problem is (3) ____, where the joint is not solid. Another is (4) ____ stress, which can cause (5) ____ such as cracks in the (6) ____.
exercises.explanation: Controlling the cooling rate and heat input is critical to avoid weld defects.

lessons.title: Welding techniques
lessons.theory:
Common arc and gas methods:

* **SMAW** (**Stick welding**): Uses a consumable **electrode** (rod) coated in **flux**.
* **Gas welding**: Uses **oxyacetylene** torch; requires no flux (CO2 acts as shielding gas).
* **MIG welding** (GMAW): Uses a wire electrode and a separate shielding gas (e.g., argon).
* **TIG welding** (GTAW): Uses a **non-consumable** tungsten electrode and separate filler rod.

exercises.question: Match the welding type with the electrode/gas used:
exercises.explanation: Different techniques provide varying levels of precision and speed for different metals.

lessons.title: Specialized welding and brazing
lessons.theory:
Other joining methods:

* **Resistance welding**: Passing current through components (e.g., **spot** or **seam** welding).
* **Ultrasonic welding**: Using high-frequency sound vibrations to fuse parts (common for plastics).
* **Brazing**: Melting brass filler; base metal is **not** melted. Joint is weaker than a weld.
* **Soldering**: Using low-temperature filler (solder). **Soft soldering** uses a **soldering iron**.

exercises.question: Which technique uses high-frequency sound vibrations?
exercises.explanation: Ultrasonic welding is efficient for joining delicate parts or plastics.

exercises.question: Match the process with the filler or tool:
exercises.explanation: Brazing and soldering are ideal when the base metal must not be melted.

lessons.title: Adhesives
lessons.theory:
Permanently joining with 'glue':

* **Adhere**: Sticking to a surface.
* **Bond**: The permanent connection (mechanical or chemical).
* **Substrate**: The material below the surface.
* **Solvent**: Liquid that evaporates as the adhesive hardens.
* **Two-part adhesives**: Separate chemicals (e.g., epoxy) that **cure** when mixed.
* **Contact adhesives**: Applied to both parts and left to dry before touching.

exercises.question: Surfaces (1) ____ to each other to form a (2) ____. A (3) ____ bond occurs when the adhesive is absorbed into the (4) ____. (5) ____ adhesives must be mixed and then (6) ____ via a chemical reaction. (7) ____ adhesives are applied to both sides and allowed to dry before joining.
exercises.explanation: Adhesives offer a lightweight joining alternative for many materials.

lessons.title: Pipes, ducts and hoses
lessons.theory:
Transporting liquids and gases:

* **Pipes**: Rigid tubes for fluids; a network is called **pipework**.
* **Ducts**: Tubes for air not under pressure (HVAC).
* **Hoses**: Flexible tubes (**fuel lines**, **air lines**).
* **Mains**: Underground pipes for water or gas supply.
* **Pipeline**: Long-distance transport (e.g., for oil).

exercises.question: Match the pipe or duct type to its description:

pairs.right: Underground pipes for water or gas supply to buildings
Long-distance pipes for crude oil or natural gas
Large waste water pipes below streets
Pipes for moving air not under pressure

exercises.explanation: Drains and sewers rely on gravity and must have a downward slope called a fall.

exercises.question: Air temperature will be high due to (1) ____ steel steam (2) ____. For machines that vibrate, use a flexible (3) ____ rather than a rigid (4) ____. Waste water exits via a (5) ____ into the (6) ____ under the street.
exercises.explanation: Flexible hoses are used where vibration or movement occurs to prevent pipe failure.

exercises.question: Which of these is a pressure vessel?
exercises.explanation: Pressure vessels must be sealed and strong enough to withstand internal pressure.

lessons.title: Tanks and pumps
lessons.theory:
Storage and movement:

* **Pressure vessel**: A sealed tank for pressurized gas.
* **Pump**: Forces liquids to flow.
* **Compressor**: Increases the pressure of a gas.
* **Fan**: Rotates to move gas; **Turbine**: Rotates when moved by a gas flow.

exercises.question: What is a pump for gas called?
exercises.explanation: Compressors are used to provide high-pressure air for tools and machinery.

lessons.title: Gauge and absolute pressure
lessons.theory:
Measuring pressure:

* **Pascal (Pa)**: SI unit (1 N/m²).
* **Bar**: Roughly equal to atmospheric pressure.
* **Gauge pressure**: Pressure relative to the atmosphere (differential).
* **Absolute pressure**: Pressure relative to a perfect vacuum.
* **Positive pressure**: Higher than atmosphere; **Negative pressure**: Lower than atmosphere (vacuum).

exercises.question: Match the pressure terms to their state:
exercises.explanation: Gauge pressure is the difference between internal pressure and atmospheric pressure.

exercises.question: Commercial aircraft cabins are (1) ____ because at high altitude the air is (2) ____ than at ground level. At takeoff, (3) ____ is zero. During flight, air is replaced with (4) ____ pressurized by the engines. Maintaining pressure prevents (5) ____ and passenger health problems.
exercises.explanation: Controlled release and supply of compressed air maintains a safe environment inside the fuselage.

lessons.title: Hydrostatic pressure
lessons.theory:
Pressure from height:

* **Hydrostatic pressure**: Generated by the weight of a liquid column.
* **Head of water**: The height of water above a point.
* **Header tank**: A tank at a high level to provide pressure.

exercises.question: Match the hydrostatic system parts:

pairs.right: Supply water to many buildings via a main
Fill a pipe to remove air

exercises.explanation: The higher the head of water, the greater the hydrostatic pressure at the bottom.

lessons.title: Aerodynamics and drag
lessons.theory:
Flow around objects:

* **Aerodynamics**: Fluid dynamics concerned with airflow.
* **Drag**: Resistance to airflow (**Form drag**, **Skin friction**).
* **Streamlined**: Having a low drag coefficient.
* **Slipstream**: Low-pressure zone behind a moving object.
* **Wake**: The turbulent zone behind an object containing **vortices**.

exercises.question: Match the aerodynamic category to its examples:
exercises.explanation: Engineers categorize aerodynamic factors to better understand and optimize performance.

exercises.question: What is the low-pressure zone close behind a moving object called?
exercises.explanation: The slipstream is a lower-pressure zone that follows a moving body.

lessons.title: Flow and aerofoils
lessons.theory:
Controlling air movement:

* **Laminar flow**: Smooth, direct path.
* **Turbulent flow**: Disturbed, messy path.
* **Aerofoil**: Component shaped to generate force (e.g., **wing**, **propeller blade**).
* **Forces**: **Lift** (upward), **Thrust** (forward), **Downforce** (downward).
* **Pitch** (**Angle of attack**): Angle relative to the airflow.

exercises.question: A road car (1) ____ is a wing-like (2) ____. Its purpose is to disrupt (3) ____ within the (4) ____ layer. By turning (5) ____ flow into (6) ____ flow, the drag coefficient can be reduced. On landing aircraft, (7) ____ are deployed to increase (8) ____ and (9) ____.
exercises.explanation: Spoilers on cars reduce drag, while on aircraft they help slow down and provide stability.

exercises.question: Which edge of an aerofoil is the front edge?
exercises.explanation: The leading edge is the front edge, relative to the direction of airflow.

lessons.title: Chains and pulleys
lessons.theory:
Flexible transmission:

* **Roller chain**: Transmits drive across a distance to **sprockets**.
* **Belt drive**: Uses a belt and **pulley wheels** (**sheaves**).
* **Slip**: When a belt slides around a pulley; **toothed belts** prevent this.
* **Mechanical advantage**: Achieved using combinations of pulleys (e.g., in cranes).

exercises.question: On a bicycle, the pedals are fitted to a (1) ____. These are fixed by a (2) ____, which runs through (3) ____. A (4) ____ fitted to the shaft drives a (5) ____, which turns the rear wheel.
exercises.explanation: Bicycle transmission uses sprockets and chains to move power from the pedals to the wheel.

exercises.question: Chain drive advantages: It transmits drive over a (1) ____. A (2) ____ will not (3) ____ around a sprocket, unlike a (4) ____ on a (5) ____. Teeth on a sprocket force (6) ____ out of the holes in a chain.
exercises.explanation: Chains are more reliable than belts in dirty or high-torque environments because they cannot slip.

lessons.title: Conversion of motion
lessons.theory:
Linear to rotary:

* **Connecting rod** (**conrod**): Joins the piston to the crankshaft.
* **Crankshaft**: Converts reciprocating motion of pistons into rotary motion.
* **Flywheel**: A heavy wheel providing **momentum** for constant motion.
* **Camshaft**: Rotates to open and close valves via **cams** and **followers**.

exercises.question: The linear motion of a piston is converted to (1) ____ motion by a (2) ____. A (3) ____ is fitted to the end of the shaft to provide (4) ____. The valves are opened by (5) ____ on a (6) ____ at the top of the engine.
exercises.explanation: The crankshaft and camshaft must be precisely synchronized to ensure the engine runs correctly.

lessons.title: Electrical fundamentals
lessons.theory:
The basics of electricity:

* **Circuit**: An electrical path including a supply, conductors, and components.
* **Current** (**Amperage**): Rate of flow of electric charge (**Amps**).
* **Electrons**: Particles with a negative charge that carry current.
* **Conductor**: A material that allows current to flow (e.g., copper).

exercises.question: Match the electrical term to its description:

pairs.right: Allows current to flow through it
Consequence of touching a live conductor

exercises.explanation: Understanding these basic terms is essential for any electrical engineering task.

lessons.title: Voltage, resistance and power
lessons.theory:
Managing electricity:

* **Voltage**: Electromotive force (EMF) measured in **Volts**.
* **Resistance**: How easily current flows, measured in **Ohms** (Ω).
* **Insulator**: Material with high resistance (e.g., plastic).
* **Ohm's Law**: Current (I) = Voltage (E) / Resistance (R).
* **Power**: Measured in **Watts** (W). Power (P) = Voltage x Current.

exercises.question: According to Ohm's Law (I=E/R), the (1) ____ flowing through a (2) ____, measured in (3) ____, equals the (4) ____ of the supply, measured in (5) ____, divided by the total (6) ____, measured in (7) ____. Power, measured in (8) ____, equals voltage multiplied by (9) ____.
exercises.explanation: Ohm's Law (I=E/R) and the Power Law (P=EI) are the foundation of electrical engineering.

lessons.title: AC and DC
lessons.theory:
Types of current:

* **Direct Current (DC)**: Flows in one direction (e.g., from batteries).
* **Alternating Current (AC)**: Flows backwards and forwards (mains supply).
* **Frequency**: Rate of alternation, measured in **Hertz** (Hz).
* **Sine wave**: The shape of an AC supply on a graph.

exercises.question: Inverters convert (1) ____ to (2) ____. They must copy the supply of (3) ____ electricity produced at power stations. Most alternate at the required (4) ____ (e.g., 50 (5) ____). Not all can produce a current following a (6) ____ wave pattern like the (7) ____ supply used in homes.
exercises.explanation: Inverters are used to convert DC from solar cells or batteries into AC for household use.

lessons.title: Generation and the grid
lessons.theory:
Providing power:

* **Generator**: Converts mechanical energy to electrical energy.
* **Step-up transformer**: Increases voltage to reduce energy loss in **transmission lines**.
* **Step-down transformer**: Reduces voltage for safe use in buildings.
* **Power grid**: The network of cables and transformers.

lessons.title: Circuit types and safety
lessons.theory:
Designing systems:

* **Series circuit**: Components placed one after another.
* **Parallel circuit**: Components on separate paths (standard for lighting).
* **Live / Neutral / Earth**: Safety conductors in an AC supply.
* **Circuit-breaker**: A safety switch that trips during a **short circuit**.

lessons.title: Electronic components
lessons.theory:
Small-scale control:

* **PCB** (**Printed Circuit Board**): Base for mounting electronic components.
* **Integrated circuit** (**microchip**): Complex small-scale circuits on silicon.
* **Semiconductors**: Materials with variable conductivity (e.g., silicon).
* **Sensors**: Detect levels of heat, light, or pressure.
* **Logic gates**: Send output signals based on input logic (e.g., AND gate).
